passage:
Monday: Lalremsiami, Manoj's manager, had noticed the errors in Manoj's weekly reports, three weeks running. At the tea break Shreya asked, "Have you told Manoj?" "Not yet. He's had a rough month. I'll say something next week." Shreya said nothing, but the silence sat uneasily with Shreya all day.
Wednesday: The client emailed about the wrong figures. From the next desk, Shreya watched Lalremsiami's jaw stay tight all afternoon and saw Manoj glance at the frowns, confused. Shreya kept replaying Monday's tea break.
Friday: Lalremsiami finally sat with Manoj and said, "I should have told you earlier. Here is what I see, and here is how we fix it." Manoj said quietly, "I wish you'd told me three weeks ago. I would have fixed it in five minutes." Passing the open door, Shreya let out a long breath.

qa.q: How many weeks had the errors gone on before Lalremsiami spoke to Manoj?
qa.a: Three weeks running.

qa.q: How can you tell that Shreya felt uneasy about staying quiet?
qa.a: The silence sat uneasily with Shreya all day, and on Wednesday Shreya kept replaying Monday's tea break, showing unease mixed with regret.

qa.q: What could Shreya have done differently at the tea break?
qa.a: Shreya could have gently asked what would make the conversation easier, or offered to be there when Lalremsiami spoke to Manoj.

qa.q: How does Manoj see the delay?
qa.a: With regret, since Manoj said that being told three weeks earlier would have made it a five-minute fix and spared the client complaint.

grounding: Shreya watches Lalremsiami delay a needed truth to Manoj to be kind and sees the problem grow until the late conversation.

passage: Vinita, sit. I'm Anand, and let me tell you about Mr Sharma, our supervisor at the mill office. Prakash, a junior clerk, kept mixing up the delivery slips. Mr Sharma saw it, and I saw him see it. "Poor boy, he's trying," he told me. "No need to hurt him." So he waited. A month later the wrong slips reached a dealer, and there was a scene in front of everyone. Prakash was pale for days. Later he said to me, "If anyone had told me quietly in the first week, I'd have thanked them." I never forgot that. Whenever I feel a truth stuck in my throat, I remember Prakash.

qa.q: What did Prakash keep mixing up?
qa.a: The delivery slips.

qa.q: What did Mr Sharma feel when saying "Poor boy, he's trying"?
qa.a: Sympathy and a wish to protect Prakash from hurt, which made it easy to keep waiting.

qa.q: What could Mr Sharma have done in the first week?
qa.a: Told Prakash quietly and gently about the mix-ups, with help to fix them, before the wrong slips reached the dealer.

qa.q: How did Prakash feel after the scene in front of everyone?
qa.a: Shaken and embarrassed, pale for days, and Prakash said a quiet word in the first week would have been welcome.

grounding: Mr Sharma delays a needed truth to be nice, the problem grows, and Anand watches and remembers.

passage: It was the busiest month of the year at the design firm, with three client deadlines stacked on one Friday. Tanuja sat across from Ujjwal, their team lead, and watched him do it again. Sameer, the new junior, had missed two deadlines and sent a client the wrong file. Ujjwal sighed and said, "Oh, it's fine, everyone makes mistakes." Tanuja knew he'd been saying that for three months. She'd seen him fix Sameer's work late at night instead of talking to him. On Friday, the client complained directly to the director. Sameer was called in and told his contract might not be renewed. He came out pale. "Why did nobody tell me?" he asked Tanuja. She had no answer. Later, she found Ujjwal staring at his screen. "I thought I was being kind," he said quietly. Tanuja said, "I know. But a gentle talk in the first month would have been kinder."

qa.q: How many deadlines had Sameer missed?
qa.a: Two deadlines.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when Sameer asked why nobody told him?
qa.a: Tanuja felt helpless and sad, having no answer after watching Ujjwal avoid the talk for months.

qa.q: What would have been better than Ujjwal's avoidance?
qa.a: A timely, gentle conversation with Sameer in the first month, explaining what needed to change.

qa.q: How did Sameer feel when he came out of the director's room?
qa.a: He felt shocked and pale, blindsided because no one had warned him.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a manager delay a needed truth to be nice, letting a problem grow until it harms the person more.

passage: Pradeep had seen it coming for weeks. His friend Sahil had decided to leave their college band to focus on his exams, but he hadn't told the others. "I don't want to upset them before the fest," Sahil said. Every rehearsal, Pradeep watched Sahil nod through plans for songs he knew he wouldn't play. The drummer, Ruchi, booked two extra gigs, counting on him. Pradeep urged Sahil twice. Sahil said, "Next week." Two days before the fest, Sahil finally told them. Ruchi went white. "You knew for a month? We've promised the organisers!" The band scrambled, found a stand-in, and played badly. Afterwards Sahil sat with Pradeep on the hostel steps. "I thought waiting was the nice thing." Pradeep shook his head. "If you'd told them in week one, they'd have been sad, but they'd have had time."

qa.q: How many extra gigs had Ruchi booked?
qa.a: Two extra gigs.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as he watched Sahil nod through the plans?
qa.a: Pradeep felt uneasy and worried, knowing Sahil wouldn't play the songs and that the delay would make it worse.

qa.q: What small step could Sahil have taken in week one?
qa.a: He could have told the band plainly and kindly that he was leaving, giving them time to find someone.

qa.q: How did Ruchi feel when Sahil finally told them?
qa.a: Ruchi was shocked and angry, going white because they had made promises to the organisers.

grounding: Shows a friend watching someone delay a needed truth to be nice, and the delay causing more harm than a timely, gentle talk.

passage:
"Kishore, you still haven't told Anil about the presentation?"
"Mahima, he's already nervous. I don't want to knock his confidence."
"His slides were wrong last week too. And the week before."
"I fixed them quietly."
"And the client meeting is Monday."
Kishore rubbed his face. "I'll tell him after that."
"If you tell him after, he'll find out in front of the client."
"But what if he gets upset?"
"He might. For ten minutes. That's better than being embarrassed in front of everyone."
Kishore was quiet. "You think I'm being a coward."
"I think you're trying to be kind. But waiting isn't kind. It just feels like it."
Kishore sighed. "Okay. I'll talk to him today. Gently."
"Want me to help you plan it?"
"Yes, please."

qa.q: When is the client meeting?
qa.a: Monday.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling as she pushed Kishore to talk to Anil?
qa.a: Mahima felt concerned and frustrated, seeing the delay would hurt Anil more than a gentle talk now.

qa.q: What did Mahima offer, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: To help plan the talk, which makes it easier for Kishore to be both gentle and timely.

qa.q: How might Anil feel if he found out in front of the client?
qa.a: He would probably feel humiliated and betrayed that no one warned him.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a manager delaying a needed truth to be nice, and urging a timely, gentle conversation before the harm grows.

passage: Looking back on last year, I think I watched a kind person do an unkind thing. I'm Nitin. Aditi, our team lead, is the gentlest manager I've ever had. When our new hire, Farhan, kept missing the data checks, she fixed them herself at night. "He's trying. I don't want to crush him," she told me. Three months went by, then six. I watched Farhan grow more confident and the errors grow bigger. I thought about saying something to Aditi and didn't, which I also regret. At the half-year review the client complained, and Farhan was taken off the account. He looked stunned. "Why did nobody tell me?" he asked in the corridor. Aditi's face crumpled. A ten-minute talk in month one would have hurt far less than that.

qa.q: What did Aditi do when Farhan missed the data checks?
qa.a: She fixed them herself at night.

qa.q: What does Nitin feel looking back on staying quiet?
qa.a: Nitin feels regret, having watched the problem grow and choosing not to say anything to Aditi either.

qa.q: What could Aditi have tried in the first month?
qa.a: A short, gentle talk showing Farhan one missed check and how to catch it, which would have hurt far less than losing the account.

qa.q: How did Farhan experience the half-year review?
qa.a: He was stunned and hurt, asking why nobody had told him, since he had grown more confident while the errors grew.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching a kind manager delay a needed truth until the problem grows and hurts more than a timely talk would have.
